1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: The natural defence: Black protects the pawn with a developing move and mirrors White's set-up. It keeps everything solid and symmetrical, and the fight is over the squares in the centre, with White usually choosing between a quiet and a more ambitious plan.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 e4.strategy: Grabs space at once and attacks the knight on f3, which has to move. The pawn is pushed beyond its supports, though, and can become a target: Black is staking its centre pawn on being able to defend it, so the move is sharp and offbeat.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 d6.strategy: Defends e5 with a pawn and opens the bishop on c8. It keeps the knight on b8 free to choose its square, but it is passive: White can challenge the centre with a pawn break at once, and Black must defend a slightly cramped position.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 e4 4.Ng5.strategy: Answers the pawn thrust by moving the attacked knight with a new attack: e4 is now hit twice, by the knights on c3 and g5, and defended only by the knight on f6. Black must defend the pawn, counter or offer a gambit.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 e4 4.Nd4.strategy: Answers the pawn thrust by stepping to d4, where the knight is central and eyes b5 and f5. The pawn on e4 is attacked by the knight on c3 and defended by the knight on f6, so Black has to keep it supported while White develops freely.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 e4 4.Ng1.strategy: Retreats the attacked knight all the way home. It loses time and gives Black a free hand to build on the space the e4 pawn has won, but nothing is lost: the pawn on e4 is attacked by the knight on c3 and Black must keep it defended. A safe but passive way to avoid the complications.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 e4 4.Ng5 c6.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Adhiban Gambit
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 e4 4.Ng5 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5, so that a knight taking on e4 is hit at once, instead of defending the pawn directly. Black may give up the pawn for development and central play, and the position stays balanced. Offbeat, but the most reliable answer to the threat on e4.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 e4 4.Ng5 b5.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Bellon Gambit
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 e4 4.Ng5 b5.strategy: Counterattacks the c4-pawn, so a capture on e4 can be answered by ...bxc4 and the material stays level. The advance loosens the queenside and develops nothing, so it is playable but less solid than preparing ...d5 with ...c6.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 e4 4.Ng5 Ng4.name: English Opening: King's English, Erbenheimer Gambit
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 e4 4.Ng5 Ng4.strategy: Leaves the pawn on e4 without any defender: it is attacked by the knights on c3 and g5, so White simply takes it. The knight on g4 eyes f2 and h2, but the king guards f2 and White can chase it away with h3.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 e4 4.Ng5 Bb4.strategy: Attacks the c3-knight, but it is not pinned, since the d2-pawn stands between the bishop and the king, so 5.Ncxe4 simply takes the pawn. Black gets some activity but too little for it.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3.strategy: Prepares the bishop on the long diagonal and early castling, adding pressure on d5 and on Black's queenside. The usual way to develop in this position: solid and flexible, with a king safe behind the fianchetto.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.e4.name: English Opening: Four Knights System, Nimzowitsch Variation
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.e4.strategy: Takes the centre at once with the pawn, controlling d5 and f5 and gaining space. The price is d4, which no White pawn covers and which Black's knights can use, so White commits to a game with more space and a hole.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.d3.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Flexible Line
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.d3.strategy: A flexible, solid move: it prepares to support a later advance of the e-pawn and frees the c1-bishop without committing the kingside pawns or the king's bishop. White keeps its options open and builds up slowly.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.e3.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Quiet Line
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.e3.strategy: A quiet move that supports d4, frees the king's bishop and keeps the pawn structure compact. It is less ambitious than taking space with the e-pawn, but gives White a sound position in which it can meet ...Bb4 calmly.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.d4.strategy: Challenges the centre at once, opening the game while White's pieces are still undeveloped. Black gets easy development and an open game, so White gives up the quiet build-up that this opening usually aims for.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.a3.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Korchnoi Line
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.a3.strategy: Takes b4 away from Black's bishop and prepares queenside expansion with the b-pawn. A useful but slow move: White spends a tempo on an edge pawn while Black develops freely.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.d4 exd4.strategy: Takes the pawn and opens the game: Black trades the e-pawn for White's d-pawn, which gives easy development and removes White's central tension. The piece that recaptures on d4 stands centrally but becomes a target for Black's pieces.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.d4 e4.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Bradley Beach Variation
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.d4 e4.strategy: Advances instead of taking: Black gains space and attacks the knight on f3. The pawn cramps White, but it can become a target for the knight on c3, and Black has to keep it defended and avoid being overextended.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.d4 Nxd4.strategy: Trades off the knight on d4 and opens the game, but White's queen then recaptures in the centre and eyes the knight on f6 while developing quickly. Black has simplified at the cost of the piece that pressured the centre: playable, but it hands White easy development.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: Recaptures with a piece, centralising the knight and keeping the pawn structure intact. Black's knight challenges it at once, and the open d-file gives White easy development and an active game.

Hits the knight on f6 and heads for a trade that puts a pawn on d5, cramping the knight on c6, while the pawn on d4 is attacked twice and can be won back. Playable but second-rate: it spends time on a knight that will be traded instead of recapturing at once.

Adds a third attacker to the d4-pawn, but the knight leaves the centre and ...Bb4+ at once checks the king. Black keeps the extra pawn with a gain of time, while White's knight stands out of play on b5.
Pins the knight on c3 to the king: with the d-pawn gone, nothing stands on d2. Black develops with tempo and ties down White's pieces, putting pressure on the centre before White can untangle.
Trades the active knight at once. White's queen recaptures in the centre and eyes the knight on f6, so Black gets a simplified position but loses time, and White's queen and development are ahead.

Attacks the knight on d4, which is attacked twice and defended once, and so asks White to resolve the centre at once. The bishop gains time and eyes f2, but White can trade on c6 and damage Black's pawn structure, so Black gets activity at the cost of doubled pawns.

Adds a second pin to the first: the knight on f6 is tied to the queen on d8 behind it. White develops with an attack on a key defender and builds pressure on the knight on f6 before Black can untangle.

Trades White's best-placed knight for the one on c6, hoping to damage Black's pawns on the recapture. But the knight on c3 stays pinned against the king and White's development lags, so Black gets easy play: a clarifying trade, not a plan for an advantage.

Pulls the knight back, undoing White's own gain of time while the knight on c3 stays pinned to the king. Black has an easy game: taking on c3 to double White's pawns, or castling with a lead in development.

Puts the question to the bishop at once and gains a tempo: it must trade on f6, keep the pin from h4 or retreat. Black loosens nothing important on the kingside and makes White decide how to treat the pin.

Takes the knight at once, so that bxc3 leaves White with doubled c-pawns, and trades the bishop pair for that damage. The pin on f6 stays, so Black must still deal with the bishop on g5, but White's pawn structure is the long-term cost.

Trades off White's central knight before it can be supported, and Qxd4 then attacks the pinned knight on f6 a second time. The knight is defended by the queen and the g7 pawn, so it holds, but White has the more active pieces.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.e3 Bb4.strategy: Attacks the knight that guards d5 and e4: Black wants to trade it, either to double White's pawns or to remove a central defender. The bishop develops with a threat and puts a question to White's set-up.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.e3 d5.strategy: Strikes at White's c-pawn at once instead of pinning. After the exchange on d5 the d7 square is empty, so Bb5 pins the knight on c6 to the king and the e5 pawn needs care, since Nxe5 is threatened. Black gets active pieces and an open centre in return.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.e3 Be7.strategy: Develops modestly and prepares castling, keeping the e5 pawn solid and avoiding any trade on c3. Black gives up the chance to pin the knight on c3 and leaves White free to choose how to build the centre.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.e3 Bb4 5.Q.strategy: Protects the knight on c3, so a trade on c3 can be answered with the queen and White's pawns stay intact. The queen also lines up on the c-file and the h7-b1 diagonal while White keeps the bishop pair in view.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.e3 Bb4 5.a.strategy: Asks the bishop to decide, but ...Bxc3 takes the knight at once and either recapture leaves White with doubled c-pawns. The bishop pair is poor compensation, and a tempo on a rook-pawn move leaves development standing still.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.e3 Bb4 5.d.strategy: Opens the centre at once, but the d-pawn leaves d2, so the knight on c3 is pinned to the king and White has not castled. After the exchanges the open e-file gives Black checks, so the move is double-edged and White's development lags behind.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.e3 Bb4 5.Q.strategy: Completes development and keeps the tension on c3, with the bishop still bearing on the knight. Black leaves White to decide how to resolve the question while the king is safe.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.e3 Bb4 5.Q.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Quiet Line
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.e3 Bb4 5.Q.strategy: Trades the bishop for the knight, but the queen recaptures and White's pawns stay intact. Black gives up the bishop pair and gets no structural gain for it.

Supports e5 solidly and frees the bishop on c8, keeping the bishop on b4 aimed at the knight. The set-up is compact and safe but passive: Black commits the d-pawn before castling and leaves White to choose the plan.

Moves the attacked knight into the centre, where it hits the bishop on b4 and the knight on f6. If Black trades on d5, the recapture with the c-pawn attacks the knight on c6 and gives White space in the centre.

Puts the question to the bishop: after Bxc3 the queen recaptures, so White keeps the two bishops with the pawns intact. A quiet, positional route that avoids the sharp play of Nd5 and keeps the bishop pair as its long-term trump.

Develops the kingside and prepares castling without taking a stand on the bishop: the knight on c3 is defended by the queen and two pawns. Solid but unambitious, it leaves Black to complete development and choose whether to trade on c3.

Leaves the strong knight on d5 alone and puts a second guard on e5, so that the trade on b4, which pulls the c6 knight away, does not leave the pawn short. Black keeps the bishop and the tension; the cost is that White decides when to cash in on b4 or f6.

Trades off the strong knight at once. After cxd5 the pawn and the queen on the c-file both attack the knight on c6, so Black must spend time moving it while White gains space and the initiative. Level, but White sets the pace.

Retreats the bishop, but Nxe7+ trades it anyway and Black must recapture with the queen: a knight recapture leaves e5 unguarded and the pawn falls to Nxe5. Black swaps the active bishop for White's knight and stays passive.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 Bb4.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 Bb4.strategy: Aims at the knight on c3, which guards d5 and e4, and threatens to trade it off and double White's pawns. Black fights for the centre squares and can castle at once; the cost is that the bishop may have to be given up for the knight, handing White the bishop pair.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 d5.strategy: Counterattacks the c4 pawn and the centre at once. Black gives up the d-pawn for White's c-pawn and gets open lines and active pieces, while White's bishop gains scope on the long diagonal as the position opens. A direct, principled way to play for equality.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 Bc5.strategy: A quieter development: the bishop points at f2 and stays out of reach of a trade on c3. But it asks White no question, so White completes development unhurried and chooses the central set-up; Black has a sound, flexible position and no pressure.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 Bb4 5.B.strategy: Completes the fianchetto, putting the bishop on the long diagonal where it will bear on the centre once the knight on f3 moves, and prepares castling. White accepts the doubled pawns on c3 in return for the bishop pair and open lines.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 Bb4 5.N.strategy: Jumps into the centre at once, hitting the bishop and the knight on f6. If Black trades, cxd5 attacks the c6 knight, but ...e4 then hits the knight on f3: both sides have a piece attacked and a tactical melee follows, with no clear gain for White.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 Bb4 5.Q.strategy: Defends the knight on c3 so that a trade there can be met with Qxc3 and White's pawns stay intact. It keeps the bishop pair in view, but the queen comes out early and the king's bishop is still undeveloped.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 Bb4 5.B.strategy: Takes the knight to double White's c-pawns, at the price of the bishop pair. The structural damage is real but small, and White's two bishops and open lines make up for it, so the trade is playable rather than best.

The natural move: Black puts the king to safety and leaves White to resolve the tension on c3, instead of committing to a trade or a pawn push. The bishop still bears on the knight, and the e-pawn keeps the option of advancing against the knight on f3.

Kicks the knight on f3 and grabs space, but the pawn cannot be held. After 6.Ng5 it is attacked by the knights on c3 and g5 and by the bishop on g2, and the knight on f6 alone defends it, so White wins a pawn.

Recaptures with the d-pawn, which opens the d-file for the queen and the diagonal for the c1 bishop, while the pawn on c3 keeps Black's knights off d4 and b4. The doubled c-pawns are a long-term weakness, but White has the two bishops in return.

Recaptures with the b-pawn, which keeps the d-pawn at home and opens the b-file for the rook. White keeps the two bishops and a flexible centre, at the price of doubled, weak queenside pawns and a bishop on c1 that is slow to come out.
Ignores the bishop on c3: White has just lost a knight, and castling does not win it back. The bishop is attacked only by pawns, but it can simply retreat, so Black keeps the extra piece.

Shores up e5 solidly and frees the c8 bishop, accepting a slightly passive but safe position. With the bishop pair gone, Black aims for a firm centre and plays against the doubled c-pawns, which are the long-term target.

Adds a second guard to e5 and prepares castling, keeping the position flexible. The queen stands awkwardly on the same line as the knight, though: Bg5 pins the knight on f6 to it, and Black has to spend time on that.
Takes g5 away from the bishop and knight before they can arrive, so no pin on f6 can appear. A useful precaution, but it spends a move on the wing while the centre and the e5 pawn still need support.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 Bc5 5.d.strategy: Controls e4, so the attacking push ...e4 can no longer drive the knight away, and frees the c1 bishop. White chooses a solid, flexible set-up and keeps the central break for later; in return Black has time to organise his pieces freely.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 Bc5 5.B.strategy: Puts the bishop on its natural diagonal and prepares castling, keeping the position flexible. White accepts a slow, manoeuvring game in which Black's bishop on c5 eyes f2, but the compact set-up gives Black little to attack and White many plans.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 Bc5 5.N.strategy: Takes the pawn and invites ...Nxe5, after which d4 attacks bishop and knight at once. Black parries by retreating the bishop to d6, guarding the knight and recapturing the pawn, so material comes out level and the game opens up with chances for both sides.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 Bc5 5.d.strategy: Supports e5 and the c5 bishop in a single move and opens the diagonal of the c8 bishop. Black chooses a compact structure that is hard to attack, and the game becomes a slow manoeuvring one with chances for both sides.

Castles at once, getting the king out of the centre before White's fianchetto bishop arrives and leaving the d-pawn flexible. Solid and natural; it commits Black to a quiet game in which the bishop on c5 stays active.
Takes g5 away from White's pieces, so no bishop pin on the f6 knight can arrive. A sensible precaution, but it is a pawn move on the wing while Black's king is still in the centre.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 Bc5 5.d.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with .. d6
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 Bc5 5.d.strategy: Puts the bishop on its natural diagonal and prepares castling. Both sides now have compact set-ups with little to attack, so the game is decided by who finds the better plan, often a pawn break in the centre or on the queenside.
Pins the knight on f6 to the queen. The pin is more an annoyance than a plan: the bishop can be driven away or traded for the knight, which relieves Black, and White has not yet castled.
Prepares b4 to drive the bishop off c5 and gain queenside space. It costs a move without developing a piece, and Black can stop the advance by pushing the a-pawn.

The natural move: the king is safe and a rook is developed, while all plans stay open. A flexible choice rather than a sharp one: Black can decide later whether to strike in the centre or to play on the queenside.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 Bc5 5.d.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with .. d6, a6
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 Bc5 5.d.strategy: A useful waiting move: it takes b5 away from the knight on c3 and gives the bishop a retreat on a7 away from any harassment. Black delays castling to see what White does, at the cost of a tempo on a wing where nothing is happening yet.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 Bc5 5.d.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with .. d6, h6
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 Bc5 5.d.strategy: Takes g5 away from White's bishop and knight, so the knight on f6 cannot be pinned against the queen. The price is a tempo and a loosened kingside while Black has not yet castled; playable but slow.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 d5 5.cx.strategy: Takes at once, trading the c-pawn for Black's centre pawn and opening the c-file. White's pieces then fight for d5, and the game opens up, which suits the side that is better developed.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 d5 5.Nx.strategy: Takes the pawn and offers a trade, but 5...e4 hits the f3-knight at once while the d5-knight is still attacked. White's knight has to retreat, Black recaptures on d5 with a strong pawn on e4, and White's pieces end up awkwardly placed.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 d5 5.d3.strategy: Supports e4 and keeps the position closed, but gives up the c4-pawn: 5...dxc4 wins it, and White cannot get it back without further concessions. Black keeps the extra pawn and a comfortable game.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 d5 5.cx.strategy: Recaptures with a developing move and keeps the e5 pawn safe. The knight on d5 is a strong central piece but is attacked by the knight on c3, so Black accepts that it will be traded or have to move, and plays for active pieces and equality.
Hangs the queen: the knight on c3 simply takes it, and the recapture with the knight on f6 returns only a knight.

Hits d5 a third time instead of recapturing, but White's a3 chases the knight at once. After the trade on d5 only the queen can recapture safely, since a knight recapture leaves e5 hanging to Nxe5; Black has lost a tempo and brought the queen out early.

Completes the fianchetto and prepares castling. The bishop's diagonal is blocked by the knight on f3 for the moment, but it will bear on the centre once that piece moves, while the knight on c3 already pressures d5.

Trades the centralised knight for White's own: Black's queen recaptures on d5, active but needing care, and White keeps the easier development with the bishop on g2 to come. A simple continuation without the tension of keeping both knights.

Guards d4 but leaves d3 weak. ...Ndb4 threatens ...Nd3+, a check that also attacks the c1-bishop, so White's king is dragged to e2 or the c1-bishop is traded for a knight, and nothing is developed meanwhile.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 d5 5.cx.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 d5 5.cx.strategy: Retreats the knight rather than trade it, avoiding exchanges that would help White's development, and from b6 it watches the d5 and c4 squares. The tempo spent is the price; Black gets a sound, flexible position and time to develop and castle.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 d5 5.cx.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Bc5
1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 d5 5.cx.strategy: Develops the bishop towards f2 and leaves the knight on d5, since a trade there lets the queen recapture into the centre. Active and sound, but it commits the queen to the centre early, so it asks for more accuracy than the retreat.

Trades the centralised knight for White's and lets White choose the recapture: bxc3 gives White doubled pawns but a broad centre, dxc3 offers the queens. Sound, but Black spends its most active piece on a trade.
